problem:
A body of mass $40\,\text{kg}$ falls vertically downward. Let $v$ be its velocity, with downward taken as the positive direction.
The air resistance on the body is proportional to the square of its velocity and acts in the opposite direction to the direction of motion.
At a particular moment during the fall, the body's velocity is $2\sqrt{5}\,\text{m/s}$ and its instantaneous acceleration is $\frac{49}{10}\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}.$

What is the terminal velocity ${v}_{\text{term}}$ of the body? Assume the acceleration due to gravity is $g=9.8\,{\text{m/s}}^{2},$ and the only forces acting on the ball are the weight due to gravity and drag. 

Express your answer in the form $a\sqrt{b},$ where $a$ and $b$ are integers.

${v}_{\text{term}}=$
{{field-1}}
$\text{m/s}$

feedback.problem:
A package of mass $100\,\text{kg}$ falls vertically downward. Let $v$ be its velocity, with downward taken as the positive direction.
The air resistance on the package is proportional to the square of its velocity and acts in the opposite direction to the direction of motion.
At a particular moment during the fall, the package's velocity is $\sqrt{10}\,\text{m/s}$ and its instantaneous acceleration is $\frac{49}{25}\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}.$

What is the terminal velocity ${v}_{\text{term}}$ of the package? Assume the acceleration due to gravity is $g=9.8\,{\text{m/s}}^{2},$ and the only forces acting on the package are the weight due to gravity and drag. 

Express your answer in the form $a\sqrt{b},$ where $a$ and $b$ are rational numbers.

${v}_{\text{term}}=$
{{field-1}}
$\text{m/s}$
feedback.worked_solution:
Terminal velocity is the constant speed a falling object approaches as the upward resistive force (drag) grows to exactly balance the downward gravitational force.
That is, at terminal velocity (a constant), acceleration is zero, so by $F=ma,$ the resultant force is zero.

First, note that only two forces act on the package: the force due to gravity, given by the weight

$$
w=mg=100\cdot 9.8=980\,\text{N},
$$

and the force due to drag $D,$ which is proportional to the square of the velocity (and negative since it acts in the negative direction),

$$
D=-k{v}^{2},
$$

where $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality. Hence, the resultant force acting on the package is

$$
F=w+D=980-k{v}^{2}.
$$

Applying Newton's second law, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}F & =ma \\ 980-k{v}^{2} & =100a\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that, at a particular moment, the package's velocity is $\sqrt{10}\,\text{m/s}$ and its instantaneous acceleration is $\frac{49}{25}\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}.$ Substituting these values into the above, we can solve for $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}980-k\cdot {(\sqrt{10})}^{2} & =100\cdot \frac{49}{25} \\ 980-10k & =196 \\ -10k & =-784 \\ k & =\frac{784}{10}\,\text{kg/m}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the resultant force acting on the package is

$$
F=980-\frac{784}{10}{v}^{2}.
$$

When the package reaches terminal velocity ${v}_{\text{term}},$ the resultant force is zero:

$$
980-\frac{784}{10}({v}_{\text{term}})^{2}=0\,⟹\,{v}_{\text{term}}=\sqrt{\frac{25}{2}}=\frac{5\sqrt{2}}{2}
$$

Therefore, the terminal velocity of the package is ${v}_{\text{term}}=\frac{5\sqrt{2}}{2}\,\text{m/s}.$
